setup: To understand a single thing the civil rights movement did, you have to know what it was trying to recover, not invent. After the Civil War, the Constitution did three extraordinary things: it abolished slavery, made everyone born here a citizen owed equal protection (the Fourteenth Amendment, 1868), and barred denying the vote by race (the Fifteenth, 1870). For a brief moment in the 1870s this was partly real. Then it was overthrown. White Southern terror and a Northern public that had grown "tired" ended Reconstruction in 1877, and over the next quarter-century the South built Jim Crow: segregation by law, disfranchisement through poll taxes and literacy tests, and lynching as enforcement, all blessed by the Supreme Court's "separate but equal" ruling in 1896. This chapter is the long runway from there to 1954, through Depression, a segregated world war, and a patient NAACP legal campaign aimed at one target: making the old amendments mean what they said.

cast.name: Jim Crow
cast.note: the South's legal regime of segregation, disfranchisement, and terror

cast.name: A. Philip Randolph
cast.note: labor leader whose threatened 1941 march forced federal concessions

cast.name: Charles Hamilton Houston
cast.note: Howard law dean who built the NAACP's court strategy

cast.name: Thurgood Marshall
cast.note: his student, who argued the cases that cornered Plessy

cast.name: Harry Truman
cast.note: president who desegregated the military in 1948

takeaway: This is the story of a country being forced, by its own citizens, to keep a constitutional promise it had spent ninety years breaking.

bridge: Chapter 1 laid the foundation the rest of this book stands on: a constitutional promise of citizenship and the vote made in 1868 and 1870, overthrown by white terror and Northern indifference in 1877, and replaced by Jim Crow, a legal regime of segregation, disfranchisement, and lynching that the Supreme Court blessed in 1896 with "separate but equal." For half a century that doctrine stood. But a patient NAACP legal campaign, built by Charles Hamilton Houston and argued by Thurgood Marshall, had spent two decades cornering it case by case, chipping at the inequality where it was most undeniable. By 1952 the lawyers were ready for the frontal assault on segregated grade schools.
setup: On May 17, 1954, a unanimous Supreme Court under Chief Justice Earl Warren decided Brown v. Board of Education and held that segregated schools were "inherently unequal," overturning the 1896 doctrine and pulling the legal foundation out from under all of Jim Crow. It was an earthquake. But a court has no army, and the white South had every intention of refusing. This chapter does two things with Brown: explains why it shook the world, and then explains why, for most Black children in the South, almost nothing changed for the next decade. The Court itself made delay easy, telling the South to desegregate "with all deliberate speed," a phrase segregationists correctly read as permission to wait forever. The white South organized its refusal into a movement with a name: Massive Resistance.

cast.name: Earl Warren
cast.note: Chief Justice who engineered the unanimous Brown ruling

cast.name: Brown v. Board
cast.note: the 1954 decision that struck down school segregation

cast.name: Massive Resistance
cast.note: the white South's organized campaign to defy Brown

cast.name: The Southern Manifesto
cast.note: 1956 pledge by 101 congressmen to resist desegregation

cast.name: White Citizens' Councils
cast.note: the "uptown Klan," wielding economic ruin instead of rope

takeaway: A magnificent ruling proved the courts could win the argument, and proved just as plainly that winning the argument was not enough.

bridge: The last chapter ended on a gap that becomes the engine of everything that follows: Brown had cracked the legal foundation of segregation in 1954 and changed almost nothing on the ground, because a court ruling without enforcement is a press release. The system would not move until people made it move, with their bodies, in public, on camera. The movement that did that did not begin in a courtroom. It began, the way so much in this book does, with a death, and with what the people around that death refused to let the country ignore.
setup: In August 1955, fourteen-year-old Emmett Till, visiting relatives in the Mississippi Delta from Chicago, was accused of speaking improperly to a white woman in a store. Days later two white men abducted, tortured, and murdered him and threw his body in the Tallahatchie River. The killing was, in the grim structural sense Chapter 1 described, ordinary: lynching as the enforcement arm of Jim Crow, with the certainty of impunity. This chapter is about why this particular murder, among thousands, became the one the movement's own foot soldiers later named as a beginning. The answer is not the crime. It is what his mother did with it, the Black press that carried it, and the trial that delivered the lesson in pure form, before there was any television to do it.

cast.name: Emmett Till
cast.note: the fourteen-year-old whose murder helped ignite a movement

cast.name: Mamie Till
cast.note: his mother, who insisted the world see the open casket

cast.name: The Black press
cast.note: Jet and others, the movement's national nervous system

cast.name: The trial
cast.note: an all-white jury's one-hour acquittal of the killers

takeaway: A movement does not run on abstractions; it runs on the moment a person decides they will no longer accept this.

bridge: Mississippi in 1955 had shown the country, in its starkest form, the order the movement was rising against: a system in which the murder of a Black child carried no penalty, and where the Black press, not yet television, carried the proof nationwide. The Till photograph moved a generation to decide it would no longer accept this. Three months after the killers walked free in that Mississippi courthouse, across the state line in Montgomery, Alabama, a woman who had spent years training for exactly this moment refused to give up a bus seat. The story most people think they know about what happened next is wrong in almost every part.
setup: The legend is that a tired seamstress spontaneously refused to move and a boycott just happened. The truth is the actual subject of this chapter: the Montgomery Bus Boycott was a meticulously prepared operation, run for over a year mostly by women and the Black church, and it is the template for everything the movement did well. Rosa Parks was a trained NAACP organizer, not an accident of fatigue. The leaflets that launched the boycott were mimeographed overnight by the Women's Political Council. And the twenty-six-year-old minister the community chose to front it, Martin Luther King Jr., was picked largely because he was new in town and had no enemies. The boycott made King, not the other way around, and it ran for 381 days on the one institution Black Southerners fully owned.

cast.name: Rosa Parks
cast.note: trained NAACP organizer whose refusal was disciplined courage

cast.name: Jo Ann Robinson
cast.note: led the Women's Political Council that launched the boycott

cast.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
cast.note: the new young minister the movement chose to front it

cast.name: Claudette Colvin
cast.note: the teenager arrested first, passed over as a symbol

cast.name: The Black church
cast.note: the boycott's institutional engine, not its backdrop

takeaway: Montgomery proved the model: bodies in the street create the crisis, lawyers convert it into a binding ruling, and neither alone would have won.

bridge: The Montgomery boycott had just proved, over 381 hard days, that a Southern Black community could win, and that it won two ways at once: the economic strangling of the bus company, and a federal lawsuit that struck bus segregation down. It also revealed the movement's real engine, the Black church, and lifted a twenty-six-year-old minister, Martin Luther King Jr., to national attention. But Montgomery had not proved the win could be reproduced somewhere else, on purpose, by an organization built for it. That was the unglamorous, decisive work of the late 1950s.
setup: This chapter is about building the machine, and the argument, never settled, over what kind of machine it should be. In 1957 King and a group of Baptist ministers founded the SCLC to run the Montgomery model through the church network, charismatic, top-down, organized around a leader. Against that stood Ella Baker, one of the most important and least famous people in this book, who insisted that "strong people don't need strong leaders" and championed a decentralized, bottom-up model that developed local leadership and got out of the way. That tension is a master key to the whole era. Meanwhile the federal government was tested in Little Rock, and Congress produced a civil rights law so gutted it was nearly useless, teaching the movement that the institutions would not deliver on their own.

cast.name: Ella Baker
cast.note: veteran organizer who distrusted the charismatic-leader model

cast.name: Bayard Rustin
cast.note: Quaker logistician who taught King Gandhian nonviolence, kept in the background

cast.name: The SCLC
cast.note: King's minister-led organization, church-based and top-down

cast.name: The Little Rock Nine
cast.note: Black students federal troops escorted into Central High

cast.name: The filibuster
cast.note: the Senate weapon that had killed civil rights bills for decades

takeaway: The courts when unenforced and Congress when filibustered would not move on their own; something, or someone, had to make them.

bridge: Through the late 1950s the movement built its machine and argued over its shape: the SCLC's top-down, preacher-led model against Ella Baker's bottom-up, leaderless one. Little Rock had shown that federal power, when it finally arrived, could break the resistance in an afternoon, and the gutted 1957 civil rights act had taught that the institutions would not move on their own. By the end of the decade a new generation had grown up after Brown with no patience left for waiting, and it was about to take over, not through the established organizations, but past them.
setup: On February 1, 1960, four Black freshmen sat down at a whites-only Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, ordered coffee, were refused, and did not leave. Within two months the sit-in had spread to dozens of cities and tens of thousands of participants. This chapter is about why four teenagers with no organization did, in two months, what the SCLC's ministers had not managed in three years. The tactic needed no money, no permission, and no leaders, just disciplined people willing to be hurt in the most ordinary possible setting. The most rigorous campaign, in Nashville, showed the tactic was a craft, drilled for months in workshops. And the new force the students created, founded on Ella Baker's leaderless-by-design model, would become the boldest organization of the era.

cast.name: The sit-in
cast.note: nonviolent occupation of a segregated space, needing no leaders

cast.name: James Lawson
cast.note: divinity student who drilled the Nashville movement in nonviolence

cast.name: Diane Nash
cast.note: Nashville student leader, central figure for the next decade

cast.name: John Lewis
cast.note: Nashville student who would lead SNCC and march at Selma

cast.name: SNCC
cast.note: the students' own organization, built to have no charismatic leader

takeaway: The students had sat down, and in doing so created the instrument that would force the country's great legislative reckoning, then split over what came after.

bridge: The sit-ins of 1960 had transferred the initiative from the cautious, established organizations to the young, and produced SNCC, the leaderless-by-design body that embodied Ella Baker's model. Nashville's drilled discipline had shown that nonviolence was a calculated method: it worked by provoking the oppressor into revealing, before a watching public, what the system actually was. The next phase tested that method harder, by sending integrated riders deliberately into the most dangerous parts of the Deep South, and discovered that its power was not automatic.
setup: In May 1961, thirteen Freedom Riders boarded two buses in Washington, not trying to get anywhere, but trying to get attacked on purpose, in front of the country, because the federal government would not enforce the law unless a crisis forced it. The Supreme Court had already ruled segregated bus terminals illegal; the South ignored it and Washington did nothing. This chapter is about provoked violence as a strategy, the federal government's deep reluctance to be moved by conscience rather than cost, and a defeat in Albany, Georgia, that taught the movement the single most important lesson of the next phase: the opponent was a variable. A police chief who refused to supply the brutality on camera could neutralize the whole method.

cast.name: The Freedom Riders
cast.note: integrated riders who courted attack to force enforcement

cast.name: Robert Kennedy
cast.note: Attorney General who treated civil rights as a problem to manage

cast.name: Diane Nash
cast.note: insisted the rides continue precisely because riders were being beaten

cast.name: Laurie Pritchett
cast.note: Albany police chief who beat the movement by staying calm

takeaway: The movement learned it could not march just anywhere; it had to choose a target where the man in charge would supply the violence the strategy required.

bridge: Albany had delivered the hard lesson of the last chapter: the strategy of provoked nonviolent confrontation ran not on moral persuasion but on engineered leverage, and a calm police chief who refused to supply televised brutality could defeat it. The opponent, the movement learned, was a variable to be selected. So the SCLC went looking for the opposite of Albany's restrained chief, and chose the most violent segregationist in America, walking straight at him on purpose.
setup: In 1963 the SCLC went to Birmingham, the most rigidly segregated big city in America, nicknamed "Bombingham," because they could count on its public safety commissioner, Bull Connor, to do in front of cameras exactly what Albany's chief had refused to. The campaign was named Project C, the C for confrontation, a deliberate plan to fill the jails and provoke a response ugly enough to force the Kennedy administration off the sidelines. When it stalled, organizers sent schoolchildren, some as young as six, to march. Connor turned fire hoses and police dogs on them, and it ran on the national news worldwide. This is where television became decisive, the largest third party in human history watching what segregation looked like when defended. From a jail cell, King wrote the era's central text answering the word "wait."

cast.name: Bull Connor
cast.note: Birmingham's commissioner, relied on to supply the brutality

cast.name: Project C
cast.note: the SCLC's confrontation campaign to force federal action

cast.name: The Children's Crusade
cast.note: schoolchildren marching when adult volunteers ran short

cast.name: Letter from Birmingham Jail
cast.note: King's answer to the patient "white moderate"

cast.name: James Meredith
cast.note: whose enrollment at Ole Miss had forced in the Army months before

takeaway: Birmingham converted the strategy proven at Montgomery into a national political crisis with a bill attached, and the man in that cell was not asking nicely.

bridge: Birmingham's fire hoses and dogs, broadcast into white living rooms in 1963, had finally pushed President Kennedy to call civil rights a moral issue and propose the bill that would become the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The strategy proven at Montgomery and tested on the Freedom Rides was now a national crisis with legislation attached. The next step was to bring a quarter of a million people to Washington to push that bill, the realization of a march A. Philip Randolph had threatened, and called off, back in 1941.
setup: On August 28, 1963, roughly 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. It is the single most iconic image the era produced, and the moment the sanitized memory is built around, so this chapter tells you what the march actually was, including the parts the memory drops: the "Jobs" half Randolph insisted on, the censoring of SNCC's John Lewis, the women who built the movement and were given no microphone. Then it tells you what came in the surrounding weeks, because the juxtaposition is the truth of 1963. Two months before, Medgar Evers was shot in his driveway. Eighteen days after, Klansmen bombed a Birmingham church and killed four girls. In November, Kennedy was assassinated, his bill still stalled.

cast.name: The Big Six
cast.note: the coalition of leaders who ran the march

cast.name: Bayard Rustin
cast.note: built the logistics, still not allowed to stand in front

cast.name: "I Have a Dream"
cast.note: King's closing, substantially improvised at the podium

cast.name: Medgar Evers
cast.note: Mississippi NAACP leader murdered that June

cast.name: 16th Street Baptist Church
cast.note: bombed eighteen days later, killing four girls

takeaway: The arc of 1963 is not march, dream, victory; it is dogs, a murder, a triumph, four dead children, and an assassination, with the bill still stalled.

bridge: The March on Washington had put a quarter-million people behind Kennedy's stalled civil rights bill, but 1963 ended in blood: Medgar Evers murdered, four girls killed in a Birmingham church, and in November the president himself assassinated in Dallas, the bill still trapped in a Congress where the Southern filibuster waited. That weapon, the device by which a determined Southern minority had blocked civil rights bills a national majority supported for generations, is the one this book has been building toward since the gutted 1957 act. Now the bill's fate, and the country's, passed to a Texan almost no one in the movement trusted.
setup: Lyndon Johnson is the hardest figure in this book to hold steady. As Senate Majority Leader he had personally gutted the 1957 civil rights act; as president he passed the two greatest civil rights laws since Reconstruction. Taking office, he decided to pass Kennedy's bill in strong form, as a memorial and a claim on history, and to spend his enormous Senate expertise doing it. The obstacle was the filibuster, and breaking it required a bipartisan coalition against a Southern Democratic bloc, the floor fight that popular memory skips entirely. This chapter stands on the Senate floor for the longest civil rights filibuster in history, then turns to what the law actually did, and the crucial limit even this colossal achievement did not reach.

cast.name: Lyndon Johnson
cast.note: the man who gutted 1957, then passed the great laws

cast.name: Richard Russell
cast.note: led the Southern bloc's disciplined filibuster relay

cast.name: Everett Dirksen
cast.note: Republican leader whose votes made cloture possible

cast.name: The Civil Rights Act of 1964
cast.note: the law that destroyed legal, de jure segregation

takeaway: The 1964 act destroyed segregation written into law, an enormous achievement, and barely touched the segregation built by where banks lent and highways ran.

bridge: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 had destroyed de jure segregation, the "whites only" sign written into law, an enormous achievement won through the longest civil rights filibuster in Senate history. But the act had not touched the vote, and the vote was the keystone, because everything else, juries, schools, officials, followed from who could cast a ballot. In Mississippi, almost no Black citizen could. The campaign to break that state would cost lives, and end in a political betrayal that pushed a wing of the movement out of the coalition for good.
setup: For years before the cameras arrived, SNCC organizers led by Bob Moses had lived in Mississippi's most dangerous counties, building local people into their own organizers in Ella Baker's bottom-up model, on a base of older NAACP figures like Medgar Evers and Amzie Moore. In 1964 they escalated: Freedom Summer brought roughly a thousand mostly white Northern students to register voters and run Freedom Schools, recruited explicitly because the country would not ignore violence done to white students. It was vindicated horribly at once, with the murder of three workers. The chapter's climax came at the Democratic convention in Atlantic City, where Black Mississippians' own party demanded to be seated, Fannie Lou Hamer testified on national television, and the movement's supposed friends offered a token that broke something.

cast.name: Bob Moses
cast.note: SNCC organizer who built Mississippi's voter campaign anonymously

cast.name: Freedom Summer
cast.note: the 1964 push bringing Northern students into Mississippi

cast.name: Chaney, Goodman, Schwerner
cast.note: three workers murdered at the summer's start

cast.name: Fannie Lou Hamer
cast.note: sharecropper whose testimony rattled the White House

cast.name: The MFDP
cast.note: Black Mississippians' party, offered two token seats

takeaway: Atlantic City taught a wing of the movement that the system could not be redeemed from inside, and that the liberal alliance would back Black freedom only until it cost something.

bridge: Mississippi's Freedom Summer had registered the cost of the unredeemed vote in blood, three workers murdered, and ended in the betrayal at Atlantic City, where the movement's liberal allies offered Black Mississippians two token seats and broke SNCC's faith in working inside the system. The 1964 act had killed segregation in law but left the ballot untouched, and the vote was the keystone of everything. Before a wing of the movement turned away from the old strategy for good, that strategy of provoked nonviolent confrontation would win its last and greatest victory, on a bridge in Alabama.
setup: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 is, by what it changed on the ground, the most consequential law in this book, and it exists because the movement executed the strategy proven at Birmingham one final time, with cold precision, in Selma. The target was chosen the way Birmingham had been: a county where Black citizens were a majority and a tiny fraction of registered voters, with a violent sheriff who could be relied on to supply the footage. After a trooper killed deacon Jimmie Lee Jackson, organizers proposed a march to Montgomery. On the Edmund Pettus Bridge, troopers attacked, fracturing John Lewis's skull. The country watched the broadcast that night. This chapter is about that engineered confrontation, the internal fracture it exposed, and the law that finally gave the Fifteenth Amendment teeth, ninety-five years late.

cast.name: Jimmie Lee Jackson
cast.note: deacon whose killing prompted the march

cast.name: Edmund Pettus Bridge
cast.note: named for a Confederate general and Klan grand dragon

cast.name: Bloody Sunday
cast.note: the televised trooper attack on the marchers

cast.name: Viola Liuzzo
cast.note: white Detroit mother shot by Klansmen for ferrying marchers

cast.name: The Voting Rights Act of 1965
cast.note: the law that finally enforced the Fifteenth Amendment

takeaway: It is the movement's mountaintop, and it was almost immediately followed by the discovery of how much the mountaintop did not overlook.

bridge: Selma's Bloody Sunday had produced the Voting Rights Act of 1965, the movement's mountaintop, finally giving the Fifteenth Amendment teeth ninety-five years late and converting, within a few years, almost no Black registration in Mississippi into a clear majority on the rolls. The legal Second Reconstruction had largely won. But the strategy that won it, the boycott, the sit-in, the provoked confrontation against a Southern villain, had been built for a Southern lock. This chapter is the discovery, almost immediately, of a door that toolkit could not open.
setup: Five days after Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act, the Watts section of Los Angeles erupted into six days of fire that left thirty-four dead. The juxtaposition is the hinge of the whole book: at the moment of its greatest legal victory, the limits of legal victory exploded into view in a Northern city the Southern strategy was never designed to reach. Watts had no "whites only" signs to defy and no Bull Connor to provoke. Its segregation was de facto, built by redlining, urban renewal, and policing, with no statute to strike down. When King brought the SCLC north to Chicago in 1966, white mobs threw bricks and he said he had never seen hatred worse. Johnson's Great Society cut poverty by half, a real achievement, but the structural city would not move.

cast.name: Watts
cast.note: the Los Angeles uprising five days after the Voting Rights Act

cast.name: Redlining
cast.note: federal maps that routed homeownership wealth to white families

cast.name: The Chicago Freedom Movement
cast.note: King's failed Northern campaign against slum housing

cast.name: The Great Society
cast.note: Johnson's anti-poverty programs that cut poverty by half

takeaway: The legal Second Reconstruction had largely won; the economic and structural one had not even been seriously begun.

bridge: Watts and Chicago had delivered the lesson that splits the era in half: the Southern legal phase succeeded at exactly what it was built to do and was finished, while the structural city, redlining, the wealth gap, the policing, it could not touch. The people who had been saying this for years were not new voices arriving in 1966. They were an older tradition, running the entire time in parallel, frequently armed, and largely written out of the story. Before the book can show that tradition moving to the center, it has to show it was never actually at the margin.
setup: This chapter doubles back across the years just covered, deliberately, because the single most distorting thing the sanitized memory does is treat the nonviolent, church-led movement as the whole of Black politics and everything after Watts as a late, regrettable radical turn. That gets it backward. There was always a second tradition, older and continuous, of Black self-defense, self-determination, and separatism, and a hard skepticism that white America would ever concede equality voluntarily. Its most powerful twentieth-century voice was Malcolm X, whose critique of King's program was direct and whose ideas would shape what came next. But the tradition was not only Malcolm and not only urban and not only rhetorical; throughout the South the legend codes as purely nonviolent, it was also armed.

cast.name: Malcolm X
cast.note: the Nation of Islam's voice for the urban North's rage and pride

cast.name: The Nation of Islam
cast.note: heterodox movement preaching Black separatism under Elijah Muhammad

cast.name: Robert F. Williams
cast.note: armed his NAACP chapter, drove off the Klan, fled into exile

cast.name: The Deacons for Defense
cast.note: armed Black veterans who guarded "nonviolent" campaigns

takeaway: The honest picture is not nonviolence then a radical turn; it is two traditions running in parallel the whole time, with the balance shifting after 1965.

bridge: The last chapter recovered the buried half of the movement: an older tradition of Black self-defense and self-determination, voiced by Malcolm X and armed in figures like Robert F. Williams and the Deacons for Defense, running the whole time alongside the nonviolent one. After 1965, with the structural city proving immovable and the faith in the liberal coalition broken at Atlantic City, that tradition surfaced from the margin to the center, got a name, a slogan, and a party, and terrified white America.
setup: In June 1966, James Meredith was shot from ambush walking across Mississippi, and on the march that continued in his place, SNCC's Stokely Carmichael led a chant of "Black Power." The phrase detonated. This chapter is about what it meant, why it split the movement, and how the federal government responded to the radical turn, which was to try to destroy it. To Carmichael it meant self-determination: Black communities controlling their own institutions and politics, a model SNCC had built in Lowndes County under a black panther symbol. SNCC and CORE went Black-led, ending the interracial-coalition model. In Oakland the Black Panther Party paired armed copwatching with survival programs like free breakfasts, and the FBI's secret, illegal COINTELPRO moved to neutralize the movement's most independent wing, lethally.

cast.name: Stokely Carmichael
cast.note: SNCC chairman who raised the cry of Black Power

cast.name: The Black Panther Party
cast.note: Newton and Seale's armed copwatching and survival programs

cast.name: COINTELPRO
cast.note: the FBI's illegal program to destroy Black movement leaders

cast.name: Fred Hampton
cast.note: Chicago Panther leader killed in his bed by police

takeaway: The radical turn was real and had a program, and it was actively, illegally, and at times lethally suppressed by the same government the movement had forced to enforce the Constitution.

bridge: Black Power had named the turn the era took after 1965, and Chapter 15 showed the federal government meeting that turn with COINTELPRO, an illegal campaign that ran from disruption to complicity in killing Fred Hampton. The structural problems the legal victories never touched, the redlined city, the war, poverty, were now the movement's whole agenda, and the cities themselves were beginning to burn. This is the end of the movement's heroic period, told from two directions at once: the fires from below, and from the top, the man the country still thinks of as the whole movement turning, at ruinous cost, against the war and toward the poor.
setup: The summers of 1965 through 1967 brought disorders to more than a hundred cities, the largest being Newark and Detroit, where federal paratroopers deployed. The Kerner Commission concluded the country was moving toward "two societies, one black, one white, separate and unequal," and named white racism the cause; Johnson shelved it. Meanwhile King moved steadily left, concluding that legal rights without economic power were hollow and all of it was bound up with the war. In "Beyond Vietnam" he called his own government "the greatest purveyor of violence in the world," and the establishment that had praised the 1963 dream turned on him. His final campaign aimed to bring a poor people's army to Washington. He went to Memphis to support striking sanitation workers, and there he was killed.

cast.name: The Kerner Commission
cast.note: found white racism the cause, and was shelved

cast.name: "Beyond Vietnam"
cast.note: King's 1967 speech against the war, widely condemned

cast.name: The Poor People's Campaign
cast.note: King's drive for an economic bill of rights

cast.name: The Memphis strike
cast.note: Black sanitation workers marching under "I Am a Man"

takeaway: The heroic period did not end in triumph; it ended in fire, in two murders, and in a tent city in the mud, having run into the economic structure it could not move.

bridge: King's assassination in Memphis closed the movement's heroic period in fire and grief, with the Poor People's Campaign drowned in the mud of Resurrection City and its economic demands refused. The chapter before showed the movement running straight into the structural economy it could not move. But it did not simply wind down. It ran into an organized, durable political reaction, building in plain sight through George Wallace's campaigns, that absorbed its momentum and rewired American party politics for the next half-century.
setup: This chapter is about that backlash. In 1968 Richard Nixon's Southern Strategy courted disaffected white voters, South and North, through coded appeals, "law and order," opposition to "forced busing," states' rights, completing a realignment that inverted the Reconstruction configuration almost term for term, the white Southern bloc becoming Republican and Black voters Democratic. The fiercest battlefield was busing: the courts finally put teeth into the old rulings just as the politics turned against enforcement, and white resistance in Boston rivaled the Deep South. The courts then drew a limit at the suburb line. But the chapter's hinge is that one harvest of the movement could not be walled off by a court ruling, because the vote, once cast, elects people, and was compounding into real political power.

cast.name: George Wallace
cast.note: pledged "segregation forever," proved a national backlash existed

cast.name: The Southern Strategy
cast.note: Nixon's coded courtship of white backlash voters

cast.name: Busing
cast.note: the most explosive racial issue of the 1970s, North and South

cast.name: Shirley Chisholm
cast.note: ran for president in 1972, "unbought and unbossed"

takeaway: The first Reconstruction's Black political power was destroyed; the second's was narrowed and walled off, but its keystone, the vote, survived the backlash.

bridge: The backlash of Chapter 17 narrowed the movement's gains and walled off the white suburbs from integration, but it could not undo the one harvest that mattered most: the restored vote, which survived and compounded into thousands of Black officeholders, the structural difference between this Reconstruction and the first. This is the last chapter of the book, and the last narrative in the entire American chain, from the Declaration through the Civil War, the first Reconstruction, and to here. There is no forward narrative. So it closes the spine the whole series has followed.
setup: The book began with a promise: in 1868 and 1870 the Constitution made Black Americans citizens with equal protection and the vote. That promise was not allowed to lapse from neglect; it was defeated, overthrown by terror and Northern abandonment in 1877, and replaced by Jim Crow. Between 1954 and 1965 a mass movement forced the country to enforce it at last, which is why historians call this the Second Reconstruction. This chapter keeps the ledger honestly: what was kept (legal segregation destroyed, the franchise restored and survived, Loving striking down marriage bans, the movement a template worldwide) and what was not (the structural city, the economic agenda of "Jobs" beside "Freedom," refused the same way "forty acres" was refused a century before). Then it confronts the strange afterlife of the movement's own memory, the sanitizing of King, as itself a historical event with a cause and a method.

cast.name: The Second Reconstruction
cast.note: the federal attempt to make the post-war amendments real

cast.name: Loving v. Virginia
cast.note: 1967 ruling striking down interracial-marriage bans

cast.name: "Forty acres"
cast.note: the economic promise refused in 1865 and again in 1968

cast.name: The sanitized King
cast.note: the radical compressed into one 1963 sentence

takeaway: The chain ends not at a settled triumph but at a debt partly paid, a promise partly kept, and a country still arguing with itself about how much of 1868 it ever really meant.
